title: Monte Carlo error
description: 400 particles drawn from the stationary law of the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process $dX_t = -X_t\,dt + \sigma\,dW_t$ (σ = 1): each coordinate is $\mathcal{N}(0, \frac12)$, so $f(X) = |X|^2$ is exponentially distributed with mean 1 and variance 1. The Observable window shows the particle mean $\bar f_N$ with its 95 % confidence interval $\bar f_N \pm 1.96\,s_N/\sqrt{N}$ from the central limit theorem, and the exact value $\int f\,d\pi = 1$ (dashed). No time-stepping bias matters here: the error is purely statistical (course notes, §1.4 and §5.2.2).

questions.text: What is the variance of $f(X) = |X|^2$ under the stationary law?
Half-width of the 95 % confidence interval with N = 400 (theory, or read it in the Observable window)?
Predict the half-width for N = 1600 particles.
How many particles are needed for a half-width of 0.01?
Add particles with the Particles tool (right-drag a rectangle, fine grid spacing) and check your prediction. Why do particles placed on a grid make the estimate worse for a while?
Watch the curve for a while: about how often does the band miss the dashed line? What should that fraction be?
